conceptTag: Build a brand for a local bakery
readerTitle: A new bakery has $3,000 for branding. Where should it go first?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (동네 빵집, 소규모 회계 사무소) · 이 단원의 개념 두 가지(브랜드 약속, 고유 자산)를 적용하는 레슨
insight: 작은 가게의 브랜드는 로고에서 시작하지 않는다. 매일 지킬 수 있는 약속 하나를 정하고, 그 약속을 손님이 알아볼 수 있는 자산 하나에 꾸준히 실어 나르는 데서 시작한다.
misconception: 브랜드를 만든다는 것은 예쁜 로고와 간판에 돈을 쓰는 일이다. 그리고 자주 바꿔야 신선해 보인다.

sources.text: 이 단원의 개념 레슨: MKT-02-02 브랜드 약속, MKT-02-04 고유 자산
모든 사례와 금액은 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 빵집과 회계 사무소는 모두 가상 사례입니다. 브랜딩 예산 $3,000은 설명용 가정이며 실제 시장 가격을 뜻하지 않습니다.
고유 자산이 효과를 내려면 오래 반복 노출되어야 한다는 내용은 일반 원리로만 서술했고, 특정 연구 수치는 인용하지 않았습니다. MKT-02-04 레슨의 표현과 어긋나지 않는지 확인하세요.

cards.title: A new bakery has $3,000 for branding. Where should it go first?
body: Mia is opening a small bakery on a busy street. Two other bakeries are within a five-minute walk.
She has $3,000 set aside for "the brand." A designer has already sent her a quote for a logo and a sign. It costs exactly $3,000.

image.label: A small bakery storefront between two rival bakeries
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 거리에 빵집 세 곳이 나란히 있고, 가운데 새 빵집은 아직 간판이 비어 있음. 주인이 견적서 한 장을 들고 고민하는 모습. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: What should Mia decide first?
body: Most of her future customers are commuters walking to the train between 7 and 8 a.m. The other two bakeries open at 8.
Where should her first decision and money go?

options.text: Take the designer's quote: a strong logo and sign
options.feedback: A good sign helps people find her. But a logo with nothing behind it gives customers nothing to remember. It's a container without contents.

options.text: Decide the one thing she wants to be known for, then design around it
options.feedback: This is the **brand promise** at work: a specific reason to choose her that she can keep every day. Every later choice, including the logo, gets easier.

options.text: Offer a wide menu so every kind of customer finds something
options.feedback: It feels safe. But "something for everyone" is what all three bakeries can say. It costs more to run and gives no one a reason to pick her.

cards.title: "Warm bread before your train."
body: Mia looks at her street. Commuters pass at 7 a.m., and her rivals are still closed. So her promise is simple: **warm bread and coffee by 7 a.m., every weekday.**
It passes three tests. It is specific. It matters to the people walking by. And she can keep it every single day, because it depends on her bake schedule, not on luck.
Her rivals could copy it, but only by changing how they work.

cards.title: A promise is an operating decision.
body: The promise now runs her kitchen. Dough is prepped the night before. The first batch goes in at 5:30. A short morning menu keeps the line moving.
It also tells her what to say no to. A request for custom wedding cakes would pull her away from the morning bake. She turns it down.
A promise she breaks twice a week would hurt her more than having no promise at all.

cards.title: Now, how will people recognize her?
body: Mia has $1,500 left. She wants commuters to notice and remember the bakery. Which option should she pick?

options.text: New bag and cup designs each season, so the look stays fresh
options.feedback: Fresh to Mia, but confusing to customers. Each change throws away the recognition the last design started to build.

options.text: One bright orange paper bag with a simple loaf stamp, used on everything, for years
options.feedback: This builds a **distinctive asset**: one look that customers link to her and no one else. Every bag carried down the street works as a small ad.

options.text: An elegant black script logo, like high-end bakeries use
options.feedback: It looks polished, but it blends in. When everyone uses the same style, nobody stands out.

cards.title: The bag carries the promise down the street.
body: At 7:15, a commuter on the train holds a warm orange bag. Others see it. After a few weeks, people start to connect orange with warm bread at 7.
The asset and the promise do different jobs. The **promise** gives people a reason to come. The **asset** helps them remember where that reason lives.
Neither works alone. An orange bag around stale bread just spreads the bad news faster.

image.label: Commuters on a train platform, one holding an orange bakery bag
image.brief: 아침 기차 플랫폼. 회색 톤의 사람들 사이에서 한 사람이 밝은 주황색 종이봉투(단순한 빵 도장 무늬)를 들고 있고, 주변 사람 몇 명이 그 봉투를 쳐다봄. 실제 로고나 상표 없음.

cards.title: Recognition takes time and patience.
body: A distinctive asset only works if people see it often and see it unchanged. That takes months, sometimes years. Small shops often get bored first and switch designs just as customers begin to notice.

The promise has limits too. If commuter traffic moves or a rival opens at 6:30, "warm by 7" may stop being special. Review the promise every year. Keep the asset unless there is a strong reason to change it.

cards.title: Now it's a bookkeeping firm.
body: Jon runs a three-person bookkeeping firm for small offices. Clients complain that their last bookkeeper always sent monthly numbers late. Which line should Jon build his brand on?

options.feedback: Every competitor says this. It sounds safe but gives a client no specific reason to switch.

options.text: "Your books closed by the 5th of every month"
options.feedback: A clear **brand promise** aimed at the pain clients feel. It is easy to check, and keeping it month after month builds a reputation.

options.text: "Tax, payroll, advice, software setup: we do it all"
options.feedback: A wide offer can win some clients. But it spreads three people thin and makes it harder to deliver on time.

cards.softwareNote: The same logic applies to a software product. A promise like "set up in 10 minutes" shapes what you build. A consistent color or sound on every screen works the way Mia's orange bag does.

cards.title: Promise first, then make it easy to recognize.
body: You used two ideas from this unit. The **brand promise** gave Mia and Jon a specific reason customers should choose them. **Distinctive assets** turned that promise into something people notice and remember.
**Try it today:** finish this sentence in under ten words: "Customers choose us because…" Then name one visual feature that customers could recognize without reading your name.
